title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
author: Naisha Roy
content:
The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for
impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program
described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s
drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many
manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and
China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those
drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name
medications they are meant to replicate.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/12/20251217-rxinspector-3x2-1.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**Look Up Where Your Generic Prescription Drugs Were Made**
](https://projects.propublica.org/rx-inspector/)

Last week, [the FDA announced](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/science-and-research-
drugs/fdas-enhanced-approach-sampling-and-testing) it will test more often and
identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and
wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or
how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA
would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable
for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-
safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that
some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for
years looked the other way.

“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA
standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told
ProPublica.

[A ProPublica investigation last year](https://www.propublica.org/series/rx-
roulette) found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves
to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of
Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On
its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based”
approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety,
effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on
its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.

ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both
the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories
that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were
ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to
create [Rx Inspector](https://projects.propublica.org/rx-inspector/), a first-
of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection
records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.

Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year
2025, the FDA [reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs,
the agency only tested one manufacturer](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/science-
and-research-drugs/drug-quality-sampling-and-testing-programs). All but one
passed every test.

The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve
been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin
Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University,
said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”

In February, senators also [introduced a
bill](https://www.propublica.org/article/drug-manufacturer-labels-us-senate-
bill) targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because
of similar public concerns.

In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and
how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the
initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster
and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further
action is needed.”

Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside
independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on
quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst
actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find
the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical
supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of
Defense.

“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of
regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need
to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”

ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several
generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States
and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise
their effectiveness.

“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is
fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so
much growing energy behind that.”
